summaries.summary: Speech-related BCI technologies decode brain signals for communication, neuro-prosthetic help, rehabilitation, clinical neurology, entertainment, preventive treatments, personal communication, games, and silent communication.

EEG is promising for BCI but challenging, and prior speech intent recognition mostly classified discrete vowels, phonemes, and words using traditional processing, while deep learning improved accuracy by 23.45%.

Articulatory speech production complicates understanding the discriminative EEG manifold, and few works relate brain signals to articulation, with EEG-only imagined speech classification accuracy unsatisfactory.

The proposed mixed neural network has three supervised steps and one unsupervised step, formulating EEG speech imagery categorization as a non-linear mapping from multivariate time-series input to fixed output.
Raw EEG preprocessing follows BIBREF17 with ocular artifact removal, bandpass filtering, and mean subtraction, but omits Laplacian filtering to avoid decreasing information content.

The authors reduce multichannel EEG dimensionality using channel cross-covariance matrices, reject low cross-covariance channels, and argue these matrices encode discriminative connectivity features beyond raw signals.
A four-layered 2D CNN decodes spatial electrode connections from channel covariance matrices, while a parallel four-layered LSTM explores hidden temporal features, both trained with cross-entropy.
The CNN and LSTM penultimate fully connected layers are concatenated into a single feature vector forming a joint spatio-temporal encoding of the cross-covariance matrix.
An unsupervised deep autoenoder with 3 encoding and 3 decoding layers and MSE cost reduces dimensionality and cancels background noise effects in fused CNN and LSTM features.
At the third hierarchy level, an Extreme Gradient Boost classifier receives deep autoencoder latent vectors and is supervised to output final predicted speech imagery classes.
The model is evaluated on KARA ONE, using only imagined speech EEG from 14 participants and targeting five binary phonological classification problems from BIBREF17 and BIBREF18.
PHASE-ONE splits 1913 signals from 14 individuals into 80% train, 10% development, and 10% test, while PHASE-TWO uses leave-one-subject out cross-validation for fair comparison.

Grid-search on the PHASE-ONE validation set selected architectures and hyperparameters, with gradient boosting fixed at maximum depth 10, 5000 estimators, learning rate 0.1, regularization coefficient 0.3, subsample ratio 0.8, and column-sample/iteration 0.4.
PHASE-ONE experiments show the mixed network outperforms individual blocks, while LSTM alone often performs no better than chance and CNN is biased toward the class with more training data.
The combined network improves accuracy by a mean margin of 14.45% over CNN-LSTM, with maximum above-chance accuracy 75.92% for presence/absence of the vowel task and minimum 49.14% for INLINEFORM0.
tSNE visualizations for INLINEFORM0 and V/C classification tasks show the second feature set is more easily separable, providing a rationale for model performance.
In PHASE-TWO, the network improves over BIBREF17 by 18.91, 9.95, 67.15, 2.83 and 13.70 %, and reduces standard deviation from 22.59% BIBREF17 and 17.52% BIBREF18 to 5.41%.

The mixed deep neural network investigates subject-invariant EEG mapping to phonological categories and outperforms BIBREF17 and BIBREF18 across five binary classification tasks by an average margin of 22.51%.
This work was funded by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC) of Canada and Canadian Institutes for Health Research (CIHR).
